notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Matthew 9, compiled from the approved sites.

---

## Matthew 9 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came to His own town.

- **"His own city"** is Capernaum (cf. Mt 4:13), which served as Jesus' ministry headquarters in Galilee. He crossed back from the region of the Gadarenes, where the people had begged Him to leave (Mt 8:34). — enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org
- Spurgeon comments on the solemnity of this departure: "More in sadness than in anger, he left a people behind him who had prayed him to depart." Capernaum was "His own city by the privileges wherewith he had exalted it." — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the contrast with Matthew 8:34 — there "all the city" rejected Him; here some leaders reject Him, but the multitudes fear and glorify God (v. 8). — biblehub.com (Pulpit)

### v. 2: Just then some men brought to Him a paralytic lying on a mat. When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, "Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven."

- **"Seeing their faith"** — the plural pronoun makes clear Jesus responded to the faith of the entire group (the four friends who brought him), not just the paralytic. Jesus saw their invisible faith through their visible works (carrying him, digging through the roof per Mk 2:4). — preceptaustin.org, enduringword.com
- **"Your sins are forgiven"**: Jesus addressed the man's deepest need first—sin—before his physical paralysis. Guzik notes this does not necessarily imply the paralysis was caused by specific sin. Matthew Poole listed six reasons why sin was dealt with first, including that sin is the root of all evils and forgiveness is more important than bodily healing. — enduringword.com
- Spurgeon adds: "None but Jesus could pardon sin; but with a royal word he pronounced effectual absolution…He gave this first, because most longed for by the paralytic, because the greatest boon, because the evil it removed lies at the root of every other." — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)
- Precept Austin emphasizes "vicarious faith": the four friends believed Jesus could heal their friend if they could get him to Jesus. This is a principle of intercessory prayer — God hears prayers of believing people offered not for themselves but for others. — preceptaustin.org

### v. 3: On seeing this, some of the scribes said to themselves, "This man is blaspheming!"

- The scribes correctly understood that Jesus was claiming to do something only God can do (forgive sins). Their error was in assuming Jesus was not God Himself. — enduringword.com
- They spoke "within themselves" — privately, not openly. Yet Jesus will address their unspoken thoughts, demonstrating His divine knowledge. — enduringword.com
- Spurgeon notes they did not call Him "man" — "the word is in italics in our version. They did not know what to call him even in their hearts: they meant 'this' — this upstart, this nobody." — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)
- The Pulpit Commentary observes that this is "the first mention of opposition to Jesus, which will be a recurrent theme" (citing France). — enduringword.com

### v. 4: But Jesus knew what they were thinking and said, "Why do you harbor evil in your hearts?"

- Jesus' knowledge of their secret thoughts itself should have been enough to prove His deity. He is "the great thought-reader," as Spurgeon puts it. — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon); enduringword.com
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the Greek variations: Matthew uses ἐνθυμήσεις ("evil thoughts/reasonings"), while the parallel passages use διαλογισμούς ("dialogue/reasonings"), suggesting both render an Aramaic original. — biblehub.com (Pulpit)

### v. 5: "Which is easier: to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Get up and walk?'"

- Both healing and forgiveness are impossible with man. However, saying "your sins are forgiven" is easier *to claim* because no visible result is required to test it; saying "get up and walk" can be immediately verified. — enduringword.com
- The Pulpit Commentary: the two alternatives cover the two realms of influence — the spiritual and the physical. Men will not believe profession in the former if unaccompanied by visible results in the latter. — biblehub.com (Pulpit)
- Spurgeon: "Thousands have pretended to absolve a man from sin, who would not have dared to command a disease to disappear." — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)
- Guzik notes the possible Psalm 103:3 background: "Who forgiveth all thine iniquities, and healeth all thy diseases" — here pardon precedes health. — enduringword.com (citing Clarke)

### v. 6: "But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins..." Then He said to the paralytic, "Get up, pick up your mat, and go home."

- Jesus answers His own question: the visible healing proves His authority in the invisible realm of forgiveness. — enduringword.com
- **"Son of Man"**: The Pulpit Commentary gives a detailed analysis — Jesus points them to Daniel 7:13 where "one like a son of man" receives authority (ἐξουσία). Jesus claims this authority includes forgiving sins, exercised now and "on earth," not only in the future. — biblehub.com (Pulpit)
- **Catholic view**: Orchard's Catholic Commentary says that "Son of man" here "does not mean…mankind in general" but means "our Lord, though a man among men, claims to exercise on earth the very authority that God wields from heaven. It is already a hint of the doctrine of the Incarnation." — studylight.org (Orchard)

### v. 7: And the man got up and went home.

- The man obeyed instantly — rising, then carrying his mat, then going home. Spurgeon: "He did not go to the temple with the sacramentarian, nor to the theater with the man of the world: he went to his home. A man's restoration by grace is best seen in his own house." — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)
- Clarke (cited in Guzik): "He who does not rise and stand upright, but either continues grovelling on the earth, or falls back as soon as he is got up, is not yet cured of his spiritual palsy." — enduringword.com

### v. 8: When the crowds saw this, they were filled with awe and glorified God, who had given such authority to men.

- The crowd properly gave glory to God, not to Jesus alone. The Pulpit Commentary notes the Greek ἐφοβήθησαν (they "feared / were awed" — so Revised Version), a more physical effect than the Textus Receptus's ἐθαύμασαν ("marveled"). — biblehub.com (Pulpit)
- The crowd noticed the authority "given to men" (τοῖς ἀνθρώποις), i.e., to mankind — yet they apparently did not grasp the Messianic implications or the forgiveness-of-sins aspect; they focused on the miracle. — biblehub.com (Pulpit)
- Spurgeon comments that the multitudes "went as far as they knew," but it "did not go far enough, nor last long enough." They saw Jesus as a man gifted by God, not yet as God Himself. — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)

### v. 9: As Jesus went on from there, He saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth. "Follow Me," He told him, and Matthew got up and followed Him.

- **Matthew/Levi**: Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 identify him as Levi the son of Alphaeus. "Matthew" (meaning "gift of God") was likely his apostolic name. — enduringword.com; studylight.org (Orchard)
- Tax collectors were despised as collaborators with Rome and as extortioners, excommunicated from synagogues. Jesus' call to Matthew was remarkable grace. — enduringword.com
- Spurgeon notes the parallel: "Was Matthew at all like the man sick of the palsy? Does he mention his conversion here to suggest a parallel?" — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)
- **Catholic view**: Haydock's Catholic Commentary (citing St. Jerome) notes that the other evangelists, out of respect, called him Levi rather than Matthew. Matthew, however, "to shew the goodness of God who from a publican had made him an apostle, styles himself Matthew the publican." — studylight.org (Haydock)
- Matthew's immediate obedience is emphasized: "two words sufficed for his conversion and obedience: 'Follow me'" (Spurgeon). — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)

### v. 10: Later, as Jesus was dining at Matthew's house, many tax collectors and sinners came and ate with Him and His disciples.

- This was likely a gathering of Matthew's old associates — he used his conversion to bring others to Jesus. — enduringword.com
- Bruce (cited in Guzik) suggests this may have been held in a public hall, not a private home: "scores, possibly hundreds, present." — enduringword.com
- Orchard's Catholic Commentary: Matthew "invites his new master to a banquet…together with many old business-fellows and 'sinners,' careless livers, at least in the eyes of the legalist Pharisees." — studylight.org (Orchard)

### v. 11: When the Pharisees saw this, they asked His disciples, "Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?"

- The Pharisees approached the disciples rather than Jesus directly — Spurgeon calls them "cowardly enough to speak their cavil to his disciples rather than to the Master." — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)
- Eating together in that culture signified acceptance and fellowship. The Pharisees considered this morally contaminating. — enduringword.com (implied)

### v. 12: On hearing this, Jesus said, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick."

- Jesus' proverb-form answer: the Pharisees, like doctors who avoid all contact with sick patients, misunderstood the mission. Jesus came precisely for the spiritually sick. — enduringword.com
- Spurgeon: "Lord, grant that if ever I am found in the company of sinners, it may be with the design of healing them, and may I never become myself infected with their disease!" — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)

### v. 13: "But go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice.' For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners."

- Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6. In Hosea's day, Israel brought sacrifices but had abandoned mercy. God prefers right hearts over ritual. — enduringword.com
- Morgan (cited in Guzik): "These words are the more arresting when we remember that they were addressed to the teachers of men…The rebuke of Christ showed that they did not know God." — enduringword.com
- The phrase "go and learn" was a rabbinic formula — Jesus tells the teachers they need to become students again. — enduringword.com (Spurgeon)

### v. 14: At that time John's disciples came to Jesus and asked, "Why is it that we and the Pharisees fast so often, but Your disciples do not fast?"

- John's disciples practiced fasting as part of a humble, repentant lifestyle; the Pharisees fasted (often twice weekly, Lk 18:12) as a display of piety. Jesus' disciples did neither. — enduringword.com
- This question was asked openly and directly — "they came to Him. Like honest friends, who felt hurt, they came to headquarters" (Spurgeon). — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)

### v. 15: Jesus replied, "How can the guests of the bridegroom mourn while He is with them? But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast."

- Jesus claims to be the Bridegroom — a stunning claim echoing OT passages where God is the husband of Israel (Isa 62:4-5; Jer 2:2; Hos 2:19-20). — enduringword.com; desiringgod.org (Piper)
- **"Then they will fast"**: Jesus predicts His departure. The early church did fast after the resurrection (Acts 13:2-3; 14:23). — desiringgod.org (Piper)
- **Baptist/Reformed view (Piper)**: Piper argues the "time is now" — the entire church age between Christ's ascension and second coming is the time for Christian fasting. He bases this partly on Matthew 25:1-13 where the bridegroom arrives at the second coming. — desiringgod.org
- The Pulpit Commentary: Trapp drew three points: "(1) That fasting is not abolished with the ceremonial law, but still to be used as a duty of the gospel. (2) That times of heaviness are times of humiliation. (3) That our halcyons here are but as marriage-feasts, for continuance; they last not long." — enduringword.com (citing Trapp)
- This is "the first slight hint of His coming rejection" (Guzik). — enduringword.com

### v. 16: "No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. For the patch will pull away from the garment, and a worse tear will result."

- The new, unshrunk cloth represents the new reality of the kingdom. It cannot merely patch up old Judaism. — enduringword.com
- Spurgeon: "Jesus came not to repair Israel's worn vesture, but to bring new robes…All attempts to add the gospel to legalism will only make the rent worse." — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)

### v. 17: "Neither do men pour new wine into old wineskins... Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved."

- Jesus did not come to reform Judaism but to institute a new covenant. The new wine of the kingdom requires new structures (the church — Eph 2:16). — enduringword.com
- **Baptist/Reformed view (Piper)**: Piper offers a distinctive interpretation: "The new wine demands new fasting." The old fasting was based on yearning for a Messiah who had not yet come. New-covenant fasting is based on the reality that the Bridegroom *has* come, has died, has risen, and has sent His Spirit. Christians fast not because they haven't tasted Christ's presence, but precisely because they *have* tasted it and long for its fullness. This is not about abolishing fasting but transforming it. — desiringgod.org
- Spurgeon: "Christianity was not to be an outgrowth of Rabbinism. There was to be a severance between Jesus, and the scribes and their school of thought." — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)
- **Note on denominational difference**: Some Reformed covenant theologians see continuity between Old and New covenants such that the "new wine" fulfills rather than replaces the old; dispensational traditions emphasize the discontinuity more strongly. The commentary sources reviewed here generally emphasize discontinuity.

### v. 18: While Jesus was saying these things, a synagogue leader came and knelt before Him. "My daughter has just died," he said. "But come and place Your hand on her, and she will live."

- The ruler **worshiped** Jesus (προσεκύνει), and Jesus accepted it — which would be blasphemous if Jesus were not God. Compare Acts 10:25-26 and Revelation 22:8-9 where worship of a human or angel is refused. — enduringword.com
- Guzik notes this ruler's faith was smaller than the centurion's in Matthew 8: the ruler thought Jesus must personally come and touch, while the centurion understood Jesus could heal by word from a distance. — enduringword.com
- Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41 identify this man as Jairus. Matthew condenses the account significantly. — enduringword.com (implied)

### v. 19: So Jesus got up and went with him, along with His disciples.

- "Jesus does as we pray, and we follow as he leads" (Spurgeon). — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)

### vv. 20–21: Suddenly a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His cloak. She said to herself, "If only I touch His cloak, I will be healed."

- Mark 5:21-43 and Luke 8:43-48 give a fuller account. Matthew's account is brief, "being only intent upon recording the miracle" (Poole). — enduringword.com
- **"The fringe of His cloak"**: These were the tassels (tzitzit) worn by Jewish men on the corners of the outer garment, prescribed in Numbers 15:38-39, identifying a Jew as belonging to God. — enduringword.com (citing Barclay)
- The woman's condition made her ceremonially unclean (Lev 15:25-27); she should not have been in a crowd or touching anyone. Her faith had elements of superstition — touching a garment was not a promised means of healing — yet Jesus honored her faith because its object was Him. — enduringword.com
- Spurgeon: "She was ignorant enough to think that healing went from him unconsciously; but yet her faith lived despite her ignorance, and triumphed despite her bashfulness." — preceptaustin.org (Spurgeon)

### v. 22: Jesus turned and saw her. "Take courage, daughter," He said, "your faith has healed you." And the woman was cured from that very hour.

- Jesus insisted on making her healing public. Guzik lists six reasons, including: so she would know she was healed by an official declaration; so others would know (her ailment was private); so she would know it was by faith, not magic; so she would not think she stole a blessing; so Jairus would see Jesus' power and have his faith strengthened; and to bless her with the title "daughter." — enduringword.com
- This is the only recorded instance of Jesus calling a woman "daughter." — enduringword.com

### v. 23: When Jesus entered the house of the synagogue leader, He saw the flute players and the noisy crowd.

- These were likely **paid mourners**. In Jewish custom, even the poorest family was expected to hire at least two flute players and one wailing woman for a funeral. Their quick shift from wailing to laughing at Jesus (v. 24) reveals their insincerity. — enduringword.com

### v. 24: "Go away," He told them. "The girl is not dead, but asleep." And they laughed at Him.

- Jesus' statement that she was "asleep" was not a denial of physical death but a reinterpretation of it: for Him, death is no more permanent than sleep. — enduringword.com (implied)

### v. 25: After the crowd had been put outside, Jesus went in and took the girl by the hand, and she got up.

- Jesus "endured the scorn from the crowd and raised the girl to life. He certainly would not let the criticism or mocking of the crowd keep Him from doing God's will." — enduringword.com
- The touch of a corpse would render someone ceremonially unclean (Num 19:11), but Jesus' touch brings life, not defilement.

### v. 26: And the news about this spread throughout that region.

- The report could not be contained, despite Jesus' pattern of sometimes instructing silence.

### v. 27: As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed Him, crying out, "Have mercy on us, Son of David!"

- **"Son of David"** is a messianic title. This is one of the first uses of this title for Jesus in Matthew, and it comes from two blind men who "saw" what many with physical sight missed. — enduringword.com (implied)

### v. 28: After Jesus had entered the house, the blind men came to Him. "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" He asked. "Yes, Lord," they answered.

- Jesus heals in response to their faith. Guzik notes: "Faith does not guarantee healing for every individual, yet there are undoubtedly multitudes that are not healed because they lack faith." — enduringword.com

### v. 29: Then He touched their eyes and said, "According to your faith will it be done to you."

- The healing corresponds to the measure of their faith — a principle seen elsewhere in Matthew (8:13, 15:28). — enduringword.com

### v. 30: And their eyes were opened. Jesus warned them sternly, "See that no one finds out about this!"

- Jesus often commanded silence after healings (the "Messianic secret"), possibly to avoid premature or misunderstood Messianic fervor that would hinder His ministry.

### v. 31: But they went out and spread the news about Him throughout the land.

- Despite the stern warning, the men disobeyed — their joy and gratitude overflowed. The Greek ἐξεφήμισαν suggests they "broadcast" or "noised it abroad" extensively.

### v. 32: As they were leaving, a demon-possessed man who was mute was brought to Jesus.

- In rabbinic tradition, exorcism required learning the demon's name. A mute demon could not reveal its name, making this case considered impossible by rabbinic methods. — enduringword.com

### v. 33: And when the demon had been driven out, the man began to speak. The crowds were amazed and said, "Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!"

- The miracle demonstrated Jesus' complete authority over the demonic realm and exposed the weakness of rabbinic traditions. — enduringword.com

### v. 34: But the Pharisees said, "It is by the prince of demons that He drives out demons."

- This is the first attribution of Jesus' power to Satan. The same accusation appears more fully in Matthew 12:24, where Jesus gives a detailed refutation. — enduringword.com
- The contrast between the crowds' amazement and the Pharisees' hardening is stark.

### v. 35: Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness.

- This is a summary verse of Jesus' Galilean ministry: teaching, preaching, and healing — a threefold ministry. — enduringword.com

### v. 36: When He saw the crowds, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.

- Jesus was not stoic or unfeeling. The Greek ἐσπλαγχνίσθη ("moved with compassion") is a strong word indicating deep visceral emotion — being moved in one's inward parts. — enduringword.com
- **"Harassed and helpless"**: The imagery is of sheep that have been cast down, torn, and wearied, with no shepherd to protect or guide. This is an implicit critique of Israel's religious leaders (cf. Ezek 34). — enduringword.com

### v. 37: Then He said to His disciples, "The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few."

- Jesus shifts from the metaphor of shepherding to harvesting — both agricultural images familiar to His audience. The harvest refers to the multitudes ready to receive the gospel. — enduringword.com

### v. 38: "Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest."

- Jesus commands prayer for workers. The "Lord of the harvest" is God the Father. The Greek ἐκβάλῃ ("send out") has the force of "thrust out" or "drive out" — it conveys urgency. — enduringword.com (implied)
- **Reformed/Baptist view (Piper)**: In his sermon on this passage, Piper emphasizes that the prayer for laborers is a missionary prayer for our own time — God's answer to the world's spiritual need is to send more proclaimers of the gospel. — desiringgod.org

---

## Summary of Key Theological / Denominational Points

**v. 6 — Authority to forgive sins**: The Pulpit Commentary and Catholic sources (Orchard) see in "Son of Man" a reference to Daniel 7:13-14 and an incarnational claim. Protestant commentaries emphasize that Jesus proves His deity by doing what only God can do. The Catholic reading, while affirming Christ's divinity, also sees here a hint of authority delegated to the Church (though the source pages consulted do not develop this in detail). — biblehub.com (Pulpit); studylight.org (Orchard)

**vv. 14–17 — Fasting and new wineskins**: Piper (Reformed Baptist) offers the most developed distinctive: the "new fasting" is not a return to OT fasting but a transformed practice grounded in the finished work of Christ and the presence of the Spirit. The yearning is not for a Messiah yet to come, but for the full consummation of what has already begun. — desiringgod.org. Guzik (broadly evangelical / Calvary Chapel) emphasizes the discontinuity between old covenant Judaism and the new covenant church. — enduringword.com

**v. 22 — "Your faith has healed you"**: All consulted commentaries emphasize that it is the object of faith (Jesus), not the quality of faith, that heals. The woman's faith was mixed with superstition, yet Jesus honored it because it was directed at Him. This stands against prosperity/Word of Faith teachings that treat faith as a force or guarantee of healing. — enduringword.com
